speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Christopher de Souza, you can take all the three cuts together.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: A Forbes article entitled, "Singapore: What happens when a nation state endorses legal innovation?" stated, "The Singapore Academy of Law has identified three separate, interlocking areas of focus for legal innovation and transformation.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: One, fostering a global perspective; two, adaptation of technology to advance and democratise legal service delivery; and three, human-centred capability-building through education and training." These are important components to further secure Singapore as a global and regional legal hub.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Furthermore, an effective and efficient legal system, a good body of legal precedents, effective international dispute resolution bodies, such as the Singapore International Arbitration Centre (SIAC), Maxwell Chambers, the Singapore International Commercial Court (SICC), the Courts, a qualified legal Bar, inhouse counsel and the Attorney-General's Chambers (AGC), make for an excellent and formidable formula for the further growth of Singapore as a legal hub.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Another important aspect is promoting the use of Singapore law.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This will ensure Singapore Law’s body of case precedents is relevant and applicable to the rapid changes in how business is conducted.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The more Singapore law is used, the more relevant it becomes and the more parties will want to choose it.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The net effect is the development of Singapore’s jurisprudence not only locally but regionally, and quite possibly globally.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Thus, how will the Ministry support the increased use of Singapore Law as the governing law in contracts and Singapore as the jurisdiction in which rights arising from the contract are adjudicated upon should disputes arise?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Civil and commercial disputes are getting more complex, with cross-border parties a now regular occurrence in proceedings.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Similarly, cybercrimes and the transitional nature of some syndicates make criminal cases making their way to Court more varied and complicated.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: With further criminological studies into how early intervention in youths can deter them from crime, sentencing flexibility is needed in our community Courts.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: How are we developing each of these legal spheres and the important partners in them – be it the Courts, the Bar, SIAC and the AGC – such as to develop Singapore into a global and regional legal hub for corporate and dispute resolution legal work which achieves fair and accurate outcomes within an efficient and effective legal system to the benefit of Singaporeans, the region and the global network?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Next, Mr Chairman, Singapore possesses a solid rule of law system for the adjudication of rights.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In order for the system to be available to all who need recourse to it, what measures has MinLaw put in place to ensure that persons of limited means continue to have access to legal aid and, by extension, the Courts and the legal system?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: After all, justice is attained only if one has access to it.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Having legal troubles is often an unexpected event, which many typically do not financially prepare for and litigation often is physically, emotionally and financially draining.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: So, when there is a need to commence action or defend a case in Court, it is common to hear of situations where the individual is financially stretched and has difficulties financing legal costs.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The inability to finance one’s litigation could possibly result in the inability to pursue justice in a case.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The Legal Aid Bureau, the Criminal Legal Aid Scheme and the legal clinics help to provide assistance to those who may not be able to afford to pay for legal advice or representation.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I also welcome the amendment to the Legal Aid and Advice Act last year which sought to enhance the process and provision of legal aid to ensure access to justice.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: It is always a calibration, but I would like to ask if there are other efforts which could be put in place to ensure that persons of limited means continue to have access to legal aid.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: On this note, I would like to repeat the proposal I made before in this House to encourage and incentivise low bono efforts by lawyers.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: We have many lawyers already doing pro bono work, but this often comes at a cost to the lawyers' earnings.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: A law practice is also a business and would have overheads and operational costs, just like any other professional service.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: But, Sir, it is increasingly not the case.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: Even for needy Singaporeans with good claims under their insurance contracts who have met the Legal Aid Bureau’s Means test and Merits test for aid.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: To belabour the point, these are needy Singaporeans who are poor enough, who have good enough claims, and who could otherwise have pressed their claims in Court with the help of legal aid if the contract had not contained this arbitration clause.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: If the State Courts have not started monitoring the type of cases, can I suggest it starts to do so, as this will give us a better appreciation of the different types of harassment happening on the ground.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan (West Coast)
text: By the same token, I suggest that the decisions and judgment of the State Courts and selected POHA cases, particularly those cases of interest, be published so that complainants and perpetrators know and will keep within the boundaries of the law.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Mr Chairman, I like to declare my interest that I am a practising accountant.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: Not too long ago, my firm had the unfortunate experience to be involved in a commercial dispute that resulted in my firm taking a legal suit against a defendant party.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: I say this, with the greatest of respect to the many litigation lawyers in this House, that being a litigant is not a pleasant experience.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: In the business world, civil litigation has traditionally been the primary tool for commercial dispute resolution.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: However, those amongst us who have ever been involved in litigation will tell you that it is a costly and resource-intensive exercise for the litigants concerned.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: The litigants often have little or no control over the process and, at the end of the day, it often produces outcomes that leave one or sometimes both litigants dissatisfied.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: The commercial dispute that my firm was involved in was referred to the Singapore Mediation Centre for Mediation as a form of alternative dispute resolution.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: This, I understand, is something that is strongly encouraged by the Courts in recent years.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: I was hesitant at the outset, unsure if a mediated settlement was possible, especially in disputes where parties were deeply entrenched in their respective commercial positions.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: I must say that I was pleasantly surprised.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: The mediation was expertly handled with clear directions and targets set by the experienced and professional mediators.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: I found the mediation format to be less contentious, driven by parties instead of lawyers, and crafted to empower parties to directly address their key concerns in the dispute, hear from each other and seek a solution where both parties are prepared to accept.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: From a commercial perspective, Sir, I could see mediation as a cost-effective and efficient mechanism for businesses to resolve commercial disputes without being embroiled in litigation.

speaker: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin (Potong Pasir)
text: In the premises, I invite the Minister to share with this House the Ministry’s plans, if any, to promote the greater use of mediation as a platform to resolve commercial disputes.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Murali Pillai, you have four minutes for your three cuts.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: On the first cut, in last year's Committee of Supply deliberations, I suggested that the estate administration process for a person dying intestate, meaning without a will, be looked into with a view to simplifying the procedure.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: However, this option is not open for estates worth more.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Since the Government has access to identity data of beneficiaries of a person who has passed away intestate, such as his or her spouse, children and parents, there is scope to devise a more cost-effective and efficient system to administer the estate, hopefully, without the need to involve the Court system.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The hon Senior Minister of State, as she then was, informed that the Ministry would undertake a review of the estate administration system after the completion of the work on the civil justice system reform.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I would be grateful for an update on this matter.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As Members of this House may remember, in January 2017, amendments were made to the Civil Law Act to enable third-party funding for international arbitration and connected matters.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Given that third-party funding can potentially facilitate access to justice by enabling parties who may not have sufficient financial means to prosecute their claims, I had suggested that the framework be extended to litigation cases.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: There is also a case to allow for third-party funding for commercial litigation cases in the Singapore International Commercial Court, particularly the offshore cases.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The hon Senior Minister of State, as she then was, informed this House that the Ministry would like to test the third-party funding framework within the international arbitration sphere before deciding to expand the categories.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: She also stated that the relevant stakeholders will be consulted, too.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In 2015, SICC was established with a view to broaden the suite of dispute resolution options here, apart from international arbitration and mediation, and further enhance Singapore’s standing as a leading international dispute resolution centre.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As stated by the hon Senior Minister of State, as she then was, in this House, the underlying objective is for SICC to be a neutral venue for international commercial litigation for parties with little or no connection to Singapore but who need and value a neutral jurisdiction with a strong tradition of the rule of law, experienced and respected commercial judges and legal services of high quality.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The diversity of the SICC judges’ backgrounds add to the strength of SICC.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Despite being recently set up, SICC has already drawn compliments from commentators for the quality of its judgments.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Also, the jurisdiction of SICC has been widened to enable it to hear cases involving international arbitration law, an area which all the SICC judges would be very familiar with.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I also seek an update from the Ministry on its review of my suggestion that Singapore accedes to the Apostille Convention to facilitate easier recognition of foreign legal documents in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Like other industries, the legal sector also has to transform in this changing economy.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: There is new technology available that could increase productivity and developing areas of law which firms could venture into to grow their business.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: There is, indeed, hesitation on the part of the small and medium firms because, unlike bigger firms, they cannot afford to dedicate resources and time to this effort in the midst of continuous and ongoing legal work.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: I appreciate the efforts with TechStart and the Future Law Innovation Programme (FLIP).

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: However, perhaps the support could be enhanced with the provision of customised consultancy services to study work processes in that specific law firm so as to make a business case for adopting legal technology and appropriate proposals on the transition process which would address the firm’s unique needs.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: I also appreciate the Lawyers Go Global programme that could help law firms internationalise.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: In this regard, are there specific efforts to ensure lawyers and law firms can venture into new areas of law?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Many small and medium firms may only be doing family law and general litigation in the domestic market.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: If they wish to access regional opportunities, they may need to develop new practice areas.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam
text: Would the Ministry consider providing support for those who wish to do so, perhaps through the proper curation of Continuing Professional Development courses?

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: The legal industry is not spared from the onslaught of disruptive forces.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: Technology, stiff global competition and growing commercialisation of the law will radically transform the depth and breadth of practice and traditional models of legal work.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: The report of the working group on legal and accounting services and the professional services industry transformation map advocate for the transformation of industry through development of high-growth areas, innovation, reskilling and upskilling the workforce boosting productivity and internationalisation of practices.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: However, much of the conversation has centred on firms and lawyers.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: Concerns were also raised on the viability of the paraprofessionals with the introduction of technology, such as artificial intelligence.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: While this roundtable discussion was only the first of the series of engagements to better understand the needs of paraprofessionals and the support they need in the workplace, the consensus was that more must be done to better recognise the potential of our paraprofessionals.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: I have three suggestions on how the potential of our paraprofessionals can be maximised in tandem with our industry transformation push.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: To accelerate industry transformation efforts, we need to expand the value proposition of paraprofessionals.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: Some possible complementary roles that paraprofessionals can undertake are innovation managers or transformation project roles to drive legal innovation or transformation in the workplace; learning and development roles to grow legal and legal-tech skillsets; technology roles to enable adoption of legal technology to boost productivity, such as e-discovery, case management and legal research and analytics tools; business development roles to understand foreign legal jurisdictions to enable internationalisation.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: To enable paraprofessionals to take on these expanded new roles, it must be provided with access to continuous learning opportunities provided by industry-recognised or endorsed training providers.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: Third, structured wage and skills pathways for progression.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: Structured wage and skills pathways can provide guidance to employers on how to maximise the potential and value-add of the paraprofessionals to their organisation and provide for paraprofessionals' progression and upward labour mobility.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Christopher de Souza, you can take both your cuts.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Chairman, in order to tap on the regional opportunities in the legal market, firms need to be prepared to explore spheres outside Singapore.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Allow me to declare my interest as a practising lawyer.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: How is MinLaw assisting firms in Singapore with ideas for technological advancement or Blue Ocean Strategies to tap on the regional market, thereby creating more job opportunities for Singaporeans and being better able to serve Singapore-based or Singapore-owned companies?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Next, innovation and invention drive corporations to better their products.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: As a result, lives of consumers are improved.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: To incentivise such innovation, corporations' intellectual property (IP) must be protected.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: How is MinLaw bolstering Singapore's already formidable IP protection regime, such as to incentivise more companies to invest in, protect and commercialise their IP here?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Patrick Tay, you can take both cuts.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: Ever wary of minimising burn rate, technology startups may be tempted to defer investments in IP protection.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: To those we have not tried to protect IP, it feels complex and expensive.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: Too often, startups end up forfeiting IP rights by neglecting to protect their hard work.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: Some simple and cost-effective techniques can minimise the anxiety and yet help protect core assets.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: This will range from advising on patent protection and taking cognisance of non-patent IP rights. ﻿Next, IP protection for the Creative Sector.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: There are more than 30,000 workers in Singapore’s creative sector workforce.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: This figure encompasses many freelance and self-employed workers in the creative sector.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: I have spoken to and engaged many of these professional freelancers in the past years through the Labour Movement.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: In fact, IPOS has worked closely with the Labour Movement as part of the Copyright Act review and has engaged the freelance professionals within the Labour Movement's network.

speaker: Mr Patrick Tay Teck Guan
text: The workers and the Labour Movement are thankful for the close partnerships.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Mr Chairman, with digitalisation, ideas and innovation become increasingly important for companies to differentiate themselves and compete effectively.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Hence, the management of these intangible assets and IP is key.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: To enable this, we must have a skilled and competent base to support companies in the protection and commercialisation of their IP.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: What measures are in place to develop and grow the talent base of Singaporeans in IP?
Head R (cont) –  , (proc text)]   .

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Chairman, I thank the Members for their speeches that were made last week and also for the various suggestions that were canvassed.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The Ministry of Law's (MinLaw's) focus is two-fold: First, we continually update the legal framework to meet the people's needs as well as the businesses', that is, all those who call Singapore home.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Fundamentally, our rule of law must remain strong.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Our legal framework must have laws that are relevant and also updated.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Second, we are strengthening Singapore’s position as the premier legal services hub for Asia, and beyond.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This also supports and contributes to the continuing transformation of Singapore’s economy.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We must continue to have a trusted system.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: I will touch on these themes, as follows, and I will begin by giving an update on my Ministry's efforts to continually update the legal framework to meet those evolving needs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We have since implemented most of the measures.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: My Ministry also worked closely with the Ministry of Home Affairs on wide-ranging amendments to the Penal Code and other substantive criminal laws that were introduced in Parliament earlier this year.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: A major focus of these amendments is to enhance legal protections for vulnerable victims of crime and ensure that our criminal justice framework addresses new forms of crime effectively.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: As for family justice, we set up a committee with the Ministry of Social and Family Development and the Family Justice Courts last year to build on the wide-ranging changes made in 2014.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Moving on to civil justice, we amended the Supreme Court of Judicature Act in October 2018 to enhance efficiency in Court procedures and allow the Courts to better manage proceedings.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: That same month, two committees, one convened by my Ministry and another by the Judiciary, proposed a number of changes to enhance the efficiency and affordability of our Courts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The public consultation on these proposals concluded on 31 January 2019.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We are reviewing the feedback and will make the necessary legislative amendments this year.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We will also work on legislation this year to strengthen the enforcement of civil orders.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: These proposals work together, and they also overlap with one another, to ensure that our Court processes continue to provide effective access to justice.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And that must remain the hallmark of our judicial system.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Mr Sitoh Yih Pin asked about promoting the use of mediation for commercial disputes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: First, I am encouraged to hear about his story and also his very positive experience with the Mediation Centre.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This vindicates the efforts of our mediation community to enhance mediation as an effective alternative dispute resolution tool.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Litigants are currently encouraged to attempt an amicable resolution of their disputes through alternative dispute resolution (ADR).

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This can include mediation, neutral evaluation or even attempting to negotiate settlements privately.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Two of the changes proposed by the committees relate to ADR: firstly, making it mandatory for parties to attempt to resolve their disputes before resorting to litigation; and secondly, empowering the Court to order parties to attend ADR if the Court is of the view that the parties had failed to reasonably consider ADR prior to commencing the legal proceedings.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We recognise that ADR mechanisms, such as mediation, can be a valuable tool in resolving disputes or providing a forum for parties to ventilate key issues.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We will decide how best to encourage the use of ADR after considering feedback on these proposals.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Moving on to the area of community justice, Mr Patrick Tay asked about cases filed under the Protection from Harassment Act (POHA).

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: These include applications by victims of workplace harassment.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Ninety-nine applications for Protection Orders were referred to the State Courts Centre for Dispute Resolution.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Of the 96 cases that completed mediation, 59 reached a settlement leading to a withdrawal of the application or the grant of a Consent Protection Order.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Over the same period, 12 civil proceedings for statutory damages have been brought under section 11 of POHA, while 11 applications for non-publication orders under section 15 of POHA have been filed.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Three thousand and eighty-nine Magistrate's Complaints have been filed for alleged POHA offences, while 51 Magistrate’s Complaints have been filed for alleged breaches of Protection Orders or Expedited Protection Orders.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: About three out of 10 Magistrate's Complaints, inclusive of those related to POHA, underwent mediation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And about 80% of these cases reached a settlement.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We note Mr Patrick Tay's suggestion to track the types of cases filed and will work with the State Courts to explore this further.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: As for the reporting and publication of POHA cases, any person may ask for a copy of the Court’s decision.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The Court may consider factors, such as whether the applicant has a sufficient interest in the action or any other legitimate reason for making the request in assessing whether to grant the request.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In every POHA case, oral grounds of decision are provided to explain the Court’s reasons for its decision.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: As in all cases in the State Courts, full written grounds will be published if there is an appeal to the High Court on the matter.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Mr Murali Pillai asked for an update on our review of the probate and administration regime.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This review is taking place against the backdrop of a whole-of-Government effort to improve the experience of citizens and also their loved ones at the end-of-life.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: My Ministry is working with the Ministry of Health, the Government Technology Agency (GovTech) and also several other Government agencies to develop a Moments of Life Digital Portal to support Singaporeans as they deal with their estate management matters or those of their loved ones in the end-of-life journey.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Features will also include step-by-step guidance on making wills and settling post-death estate matters.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: On top of that, we are also considering ways in which we can simplify estate administration, how the process is for affected families, particularly where smaller estates are concerned.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: So, we are making the process simpler, more straightforward, less expensive for the simpler, smaller cases but, at the same time, also going upstream to help with estate management and planning prior to that stage.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Mr Christopher de Souza and Mdm Rahayu Mahzam asked about legal aid.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We will continue to review these schemes to ensure that persons of limited means, the right target clientele for this scheme, will remain assisted and will have access to justice.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We are working with our partners, the Law Society Pro Bono Services and the Singapore Academy of Law, to study how we can further enhance support for pro bono and also low bono efforts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Mr Chen Show Mao also asked about legal aid for arbitration in disputes over consumer contracts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: As a general rule, legal aid is not provided for arbitration because it is a private, consensual dispute mechanism and it is typically used for high-value commercial dispute resolution.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Nonetheless, I would like to assure Mr Chen Show Mao that there are several avenues available for such consumers to seek assistance and redress.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Before consumers undergo arbitration, they can obtain free legal advice from the Legal Aid Bureau (LAB) on the arbitration clauses in the contract.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This can help consumers better understand their rights and obligations under the contract, and LAB can also provide substantive advice and also legal options available to the consumer.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Consumers who then wish to take their dispute to resolution by arbitration in a quick and cost-effective manner can consider the Law Society's Pro Bono Arbitration Scheme, which adopts streamlined procedures and, more importantly, waives the fees of the sole arbitrators in those cases.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: If the consumer wishes to challenge the arbitration clause or the arbitration award, he can apply for legal aid for representation in Court.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And LAB will represent such consumers if there are legal merits in his case.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: That said, if Mr Chen Show Mao is able to provide us with the specific case that he has encountered.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In the example he cited last week, there is a case where a consumer is in a situation where he has got no choice over the entry into the contract.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: My Ministry will review the case and see what we can do to assist on a case-by-case basis.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: On top of that, we will also continue to monitor developments in this area with the Ministry of Trade and Industry since it concerns consumer protection and consider whether further steps need to be taken.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: A number of Members have asked specifically about the intellectual property (IP) regime in Singapore, and I will turn to that next.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The Minister for Finance spoke about positioning Singapore as a "Global-Asia node of technology, innovation and enterprise" for our next phase of growth, so these are quite pertinent questions which Members have raised.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: My Ministry's efforts in the area of IP will support this push in four major ways.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: First, we are positioning our IP system to better support creators and innovators.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: For example, creators will find it easier to build their reputation as people who use their works will then have to properly acknowledge the creator.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Creators of certain commissioned works will also enjoy default ownership of their works whereas, previously, the commissioning party would own the works.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: As for innovators, innovative businesses in data analytics will find it easier to mine data for analysis.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Details can be found in the Copyright Review Report, a fairly comprehensive report which was released in January 2019.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: At the same time, we are also reviewing the IP dispute resolution system to make it more accessible, especially for individuals and small and medium enterprises (SMEs), so that they can more effectively safeguard their rights.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We held a public consultation on proposed reforms in late 2018 and we are now studying the feedback that was received from the community for the next phase.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Mr Patrick Tay also asked about helping Fintech startups to protect their IP.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: FinTech startups can also avail themselves of other assistance schemes available to Singapore businesses, some of which I am going to highlight.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Second, we are helping Singapore businesses in commercialising their IP rights.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: IPOS also provides specialised consultancy services on IP audit, due diligence and strategy to help enterprises identify their intangible assets and also integrate them into their own strategies for growth and expansion.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: About 80 enterprises have benefited from these services, with close to 90% of them being either SMEs or startups.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: When enterprises seek assistance in developing their IP strategy management capabilities, eligible costs may also be defrayed under Enterprise Singapore's Market Readiness Assistance Grant and the Enterprise Development Grant.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: While there is still some way to go in encouraging businesses to leverage their IP growth and take advantage of the ecosystem, we have seen a number of success stories.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: One example is OTSAW Digital, an SME which builds autonomous robots for the security industry.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: IPOS assisted the company in developing its IP strategy – how to protect and manage its IP and, thereafter, exploit it, as well as other intangible assets.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: OTSAW now has internal processes to identify IP that is developed and to protect it appropriately.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: It is also more aware of IP-related issues when negotiating with other business partners and also, of course, potential investors.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The company is now expanding internationally into Malaysia, Indonesia and the Chinese markets.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We are naturally excited to see them grow as they leverage their startup position, IP rights, and look forward to observing their continued success.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Third, we are making it easier for businesses to commercialise IP from the public sector.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The National IP Protocol was developed and rolled out in April 2018 to encourage commercialisation of public sector IP and also research and development outputs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: It streamlines IP practices in our public research institutes, universities and public agencies to reduce the time and effort needed to structure commercialisation agreements entered into with the private sector.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This will foster greater collaboration between the private sector businesses on the one hand and the public sector.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: IPOS has partnered SkillsFuture Singapore to develop the first national level skills development framework for the IP sector.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This will be rolled out in August 2019.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This framework will provide comprehensive information on the career options, skills needed for the various job roles, and also the training programmes relevant for the IP sector.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This will aid in the upskilling of new entrants and also existing IP professionals.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: IPOS has also partnered Workforce Singapore on the IP Professional Conversion Programme, and with SkillsFuture Singapore on the SkillsFuture Study Awards.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: These schemes provide financial support for the reskilling of newly-hired employees and for individuals who are seeking to deepen and broaden their skills.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We are also developing programmes to ensure that trained individuals are recognised with certifications.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: All these measures work towards ensuring that our legal system meets the needs of all, whether it is the man-in-the-street or businesses large or small who call Singapore home.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Our legal system as a whole also plays a broader role as a supporting pillar for the next phase of Singapore’s economic transformation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: On this, there are two interlocking aspects of my Ministry's efforts to provide this support.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: First, we are strengthening Singapore's position as an international legal services hub.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Second, we are working to establish Singapore as a thought leader of international rule of law and pursuing international cooperation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: These mutually reinforcing efforts together underpin our position in an increasingly uncertain world as a trusted, stable centre for law and business, and I would like to elaborate on these few points now.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: First, we are investing in strengthening Singapore's position as a premier legal services hub, both regionally as well as globally.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This means strengthening our position as a dispute resolution centre, growing new areas to meet the demands of international legal services, and finally, promoting the use of Singapore law to meet business needs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: There are three broad categories of efforts related to dispute resolution.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: First, we have been and we continue to position Singapore as a trusted and neutral forum for dispute resolution.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The Singapore International Arbitration Centre (SIAC) is also the third most preferred arbitral institution in the world.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And SIAC, along with the Singapore International Mediation Centre (SIMC) and the Singapore International Commercial Court (SICC), have all seen increases in caseload over the years.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: As for SIMC, as of 31 December 2018, it had received a total of 68 case filings from parties from more than 20 different jurisdictions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: For SICC, 29 cases have reached SICC since it was established in 2015.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Mr Murali Pillai asked for an update on SICC.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Beyond just the caseload alone, what SICC has been working very hard on is to enhance the enforceability of SICC judgments.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In 2018, our Supreme Court and the Supreme People's Court of China signed a Memorandum of Guidance on the recognition and enforcement of money judgments in commercial cases.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This means that parties who have commercial dealings are much clearer on how any money judgments arising from disputes can be enforced against any other party, whether in Singapore or in China.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Mr Murali Pillai also asked about third-party funding, for an update in the area of international arbitration.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: My Ministry has consulted a public consultation to obtain feedback from stakeholders on how the reforms have been working in practice.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We also asked if there was a need to extend third-party funding to new areas.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Mr Murali Pillai would be pleased to know that funders have seen an upturn in the requests for funding in Singapore and there has also been support for expansion.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We are currently reviewing the overall framework, how it might work, including areas for potential extension into proceedings commenced in SICC and any appeals from SICC.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Second, we must continue to invest in order to strengthen our leadership position.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We are bolstering our infrastructure to meet demand and also support growth.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The expansion of Maxwell Chambers is on track.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: But it is not just about size or how big the physical infrastructure is.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We need to deepen our collaborations with international institutions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And on this score, we have attracted top arbitral institutions to set up offices in Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The International Court of Arbitration of the International Chamber of Commerce, for instance, has set up a case management office here.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The Permanent Court of Arbitration has its new office in Singapore, its first in Asia.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: SIAC has also signed memorandums of understanding (MOUs) with a number of Chinese institutions in 2018 alone.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: China International Economic and Trade Arbitration Commission, one of the leading commissions in China for dispute resolution, an MOU was signed in 2018.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Likewise, an MOU was also signed with the Shenzhen Court of International Arbitration as well as with the Xi'an Arbitration Commission.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: As far as mediation is concerned, SIMC signed an MOU in 2018 with the Asian Development Bank to help resolve disputes that may arise in infrastructure public-private partnership projects, and an MOU with the China Council for Promotion of International Trade Mediation Centre in January 2019.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Further to our efforts in enhancing Singapore's attractiveness as a forum for dispute resolution, we have also identified several high-growth practice areas to develop.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: First, in the area of insolvency and debt restructuring.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We amended the Companies Act previously and now we have got an omnibus Act that was passed in 2018, the Insolvency Restructuring and Dissolution Act.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And that was the final piece of principal legislation in our phased implementation of the recommendations of the Law Review Committee as well as the Committee to Strengthen Singapore as an International Centre for Debt Structuring.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: So, we now have legislation that seeks to properly balance the interests of debtors and creditors as they are undergoing restructuring in Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The Act, which we target to bring into force this year, benefits local businesses needing help, positions Singapore as a location of choice for foreign debtors to restructure and also creates new opportunities for insolvency professionals, distressed debt funds and also financial institutions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Second, in the area of Projects and Infrastructure.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We have taken steps to capture the increasing demand for legal services in this area.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Infrastructure Asia, Singapore's infrastructure office, was launched in October 2018.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This is an office set up by the Monetary Authority of Singapore, Enterprise Singapore, and supported by MinLaw through our Professional Services Programme Office.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: It provides a platform for information exchange on infrastructure opportunities in Asia, facilitates investments and financing, and gives Singapore-based infrastructure players access to these opportunities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In the same month, we also launched the Singapore Infrastructure Dispute-Management Protocol.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: It helps to proactively manage differences to prevent them from escalating into disputes and also minimise the risks of time and cost overruns, all of which aimed at enhancing and improving on the large-scale infrastructure ecosystem in Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Mr Christopher de Souza has rightly pointed out that Singapore's position as an international legal services hub can be further strengthened by promoting the use of Singapore law.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And Singapore law is well-placed to meet the legal needs of businesses in Asia, particularly those businesses that are previously familiar with or accustomed to using English law.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Singapore law benefits from its roots in the English common law system but has gone on to evolve to remain modern and relevant.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And overlaid on our common law are legal frameworks and statutes which are often developed in very close consultation with the industry users.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Those who choose Singapore law choose to do so as they wish to tap into a legal system that is not just familiar but one which is trusted, both in Singapore as well as internationally.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The promotion of Singapore law does not, however, just involve Government stakeholders, but is also driven from the ground up, by the Bar and from others within this ecosystem.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: For example, in October 2018, the Singapore Academy of Law and the Singapore Venture Capital and Private Equity Association launched the Venture Capital Investment Model Agreements (VIMA).

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This is a set of standard-form documents which make the process of structuring a deal faster, quicker and more cost-efficient for startups and venture capital firms.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: VIMA incorporates Singapore law as the governing law and Singapore as the chosen dispute resolution forum.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: My Ministry also works with the universities to encourage research that helps to develop and strengthen Singapore law.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The intent is to ensure that our law remains cutting-edge, and not just cutting-edge, but also one that meets the needs of our modern businesses.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We continue to welcome views and suggestions from practitioners and businessmen alike on how we can further strengthen and enhance these laws.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Besides the efforts to strengthen our position as a premier legal services hub, we are also investing in establishing Singapore as a thought leader in international rule of law efforts and also participating in legal cooperation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: First, we want to establish Singapore as an advocate of, and a thought leader in, international rule of law efforts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This reinforces Singapore's reputation brand as a forum of choice for cross-border dispute resolution and also other forms of alternative dispute resolutions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We also engage actively in international efforts to design new international rules to ensure that Singapore's perspectives and our unique circumstances are not ignored.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: For example, my Ministry, together with other Ministries, worked to secure Singapore's re-election as a member of the United Nations Commission on International Trade Law from 2019.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This will enable Singapore to continue to actively participate in the development of international trade law.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We have also worked hard to promote international law scholarship, particularly in the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) law context.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: For instance, we supported the launch of the ASEAN Law Academy at the National University of Singapore (NUS) last year.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: At the same time, we must also ensure that we are a responsible global citizen, if we are to earn and maintain the trust of the international community.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: There are two aspects to international cooperation that I will touch on: criminal cooperation and civil cooperation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We are pursuing a number of efforts in the area of civil cooperation as well.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: My Ministry is currently studying the possibility of doing so.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We have begun discussions with stakeholders, engaged representatives from the Hague Conference about the practicalities and the steps needed in implementing the Convention.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: All of these efforts translate into more opportunities for Singapore law practices.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Both Mr Christopher de Souza and Mdm Rahayu Mahzam have asked how Singapore law practices are being assisted to take advantage of the opportunities created for them.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The final area that I will, therefore, cover relates to our efforts to support Singapore law practices (SLPs) to adapt.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And not just that, but to go beyond and take advantage of these opportunities in this broader landscape that has been curated.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Broadly, we are supporting SLPs in three ways.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: To sustain their business in the face of competition and technological disruption and, as Ms Rahayu Mahzam has pointed out, law firms need to venture into new practice areas.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We cannot keep holding on to the conventional ones.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: My Ministry will continue to help Singapore lawyers develop capabilities in high-growth practice areas.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: To give an example, we worked with the NUS Faculty of Law to roll out "The Project Finance Academy", a three-day practical hands-on workshop in November 2018 to take participants through the main legal considerations in structuring project financing transactions and negotiating infrastructure deals.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We also encourage and support law firms to develop new practice areas and access regional opportunities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Also, in response to Ms Rahayu Mahzam's suggestion on continuing professional development (CPD) courses, the Singapore Academy of Law and the Law Society of Singapore have been developing various CPD programmes and courses, designed in a new way, to equip practitioners interested in deepening or building practices in new areas.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Some of these programmes are also approved for SkillsFuture credits.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We will share the feedback that has been given by Ms Rahayu Mahzam last week with the Singapore Academy of Law and the Law Society.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: My Ministry is supporting the efforts of SLPs to capture a greater share of international demand for legal services.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In other words, look not just at Singapore as the market, but to go beyond Singapore, into the region and globally.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The programme helps lawyers expand their networks outside Singapore through mission trips, training and also a branding exercise for the Singapore lawyer brand.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We have also stepped up our engagements in Asia.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: My Ministry has led our law firms and institutions on promotion trips to Asian countries.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: I visited China earlier this year to strengthen Singapore-China legal and judicial cooperation.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: During my visit, I attended and spoke at the "China-Singapore International Commercial Dispute Resolution Conference", a first of its kind, jointly organised by Singapore and China.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Senior Minister of State, if you could just wrap up.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In the longer term, we will work with the Agency for Science, Technology and Research (A*STAR) to develop a broader-term roadmap for up to 2030, in identifying technologies that will impact and change the delivery of legal services.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Fourth, we continue the development of legal talent not just for lawyers but also for sub-specialists like paralegals.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We continue to work closely with the law schools to ensure the law curriculum, the training, are robust and prepare our lawyers and paralegals for future generations.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We will also continue to support Singapore lawyers to deepen their skills through the SkillsFuture programmes, as I mentioned earlier.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Chairman, just give me a few minutes as I wrap up.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I will conclude with the question that drives all of us – what purposes must the legal framework serve?

speaker: The Chairman
text: So, assuming clarifications do not extend beyond that, I am happy to eat into clarification time.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, the Singapore Academy of Law and INSEAD run a Law Firm Leadership Programme.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: At the same time, SkillsFuture also supports qualifications for solicitors to seek admission as solicitors of England and Wales through the Qualified Lawyers Transfer Scheme.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The role of paralegals is growing and we recognise the integral roles that they and other legal support professionals play in this industry.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, we will also continue to work with the Singapore Academy of Law on its programme, Legal Industry Framework for Training and Education for paralegals.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This maps out the competency and training that are needed for paralegals to move up the value chain and support legal services.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In addition, we also provided pathways for paralegals who wish to upskill and advance their career.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: As I mentioned earlier, we ask ourselves: what purpose must our legal framework serve?

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We must have a legal framework that is fair, transparent, updated and remains relevant to the users of the system and, most importantly, underpinned by a strong rule of law.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It must then meet the needs of individuals and businesses who call Singapore home.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We do this through ensuring that our criminal, civil and family justice networks and frameworks are up to date and making sure that persons of limited means have and will continue to have access to justice.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Second, on a broader level, the legal framework must support Singapore’s continuing economic growth.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This is especially crucial as we enter a season of global economic uncertainty.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: While it will pose challenges, there will also be many opportunities from these challenges and disruptions that we can reap, if we can leverage our position as a stable and trusted centre for law and businesses.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: None of this, however, can be done by the Government alone.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In particular, therefore, I wish to record my appreciation and gratitude to the many members of the Bar for their numerous contributions to the work of my Ministry.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Many have given their time and expertise to sit on our committees, give feedback during consultations, and also collaborate with us on our many initiatives, both locally as well as overseas.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I am grateful for their close involvement in all that we do, and I look forward to building on this strong relationship.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: On our end, we will continue to work with all stakeholders to achieve all of the objectives I have just set out.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I saw quite a thick file, and if there is anything more the Senior Minister of State would like to say on SkillsFuture, legal technology use in Singapore, and regional and global outreach —

speaker: The Chairman
text: This is clarification, not an excuse for extra speech time.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: In addition to those clarifications, Mr Chairman, the use of SMC is very positive.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: But at the same time, where we have a lot of cases settled and the settlements are kept confidential, it does impact the development of legal jurisprudence in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: So, in addition to the clarifications that I asked previously, would there be a move to encourage parties who do not mind having their settlements non-confidential in nature and allow for the mediators' understanding and grounds in coming to his/her conclusion published, and quite possibly published as a judgment of Court or a decision of the SMC?

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Most mediations – and I think Mr Sitoh Yih Pin's own experience has been the same – are private and confidential for a number of reasons.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: People choose to look at the dispute from different angles.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mediation allows you to explore resolution of the dispute on means which are completely extralegal on different considerations, such as commercial considerations or maybe confidentiality considerations.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, it might not necessarily add to legal jurisprudence to have those mediation agreements published.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But I understand Mr Christopher de Souza's point on those cases where there might be legal jurisprudence and legal merit in doing so.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: On Mr Christopher de Souza's first point – and I welcome that because it gives me an opportunity to explain this a little bit more – we do see development in upskilling of know-how, competencies as a very important part of legal development.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We have to make sure that our lawyers who come out from law school and those who come out from their practice traineeship are properly equipped for practice.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Christopher de Souza knows that we have been looking very closely at what we do with practice traineeship.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The Committee has given a very extensive discussion on that.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Christopher de Souza, would you like to withdraw the amendment?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: Mr Chairman, Sir, we have had a productive debate, first starting on Friday and then now concluding on Monday.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: These include MinLaw, IPOS, the Insolvency and Public Trustee's Office and many other public officers.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: So, in conclusion, a big thank you to Minister K Shanmugam, Senior Minister of State Edwin Tong, MinLaw and the officers for their hard work.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza
text: With that, Mr Chairman, I beg leave to withdraw my amendment.
